title: The Edge and BYOC Premises
summary: Premises Edges, Edge groups, phone trunks, sites, and what happens when the local Edge is down.

lessons.title: The premises Edge is the local media hop
lessons.summary: BYOC Premises puts an Edge on your network. Phones and trunks registered there do not need a public address the way BYOC Cloud does.
paras: An Edge group is a set of premises Edges on a low-latency network. Phones on those Edges can call each other, and a trunk plugged into one Edge can be used by the others in the group. That sharing is the point of the group. A single Edge with no group is a single point of failure for every phone that depends on it.

This is a different product from BYOC Cloud. Cloud trunks terminate in AWS. Premises trunks terminate on the Edge. Emergency calling can still be internet-based in some premises designs, and the same Genesys warning applies: if the call rides a BYOC trunk, Genesys is not the emergency provider.

lessons.title: Local site routing stays home until it cannot
lessons.summary: Genesys uses Edges in the same site when it can. Another site is the exception.
paras: The Edge group article says local site routing prefers same-site Edges to save bandwidth and latency. Another site is used when local Edges are offline, already at capacity, or do not hold the resource, such as the agent, the station, or the trunk.

A site is also where number plans and outbound routes live, and where you attach a location. Building two sites and one giant Edge group across a slow WAN fights the article. The group wants a low-latency network. The site wants local media. Those sentences should agree.

lessons.title: Phone trunks, WebRTC, and inherit
lessons.summary: WebRTC and SIP phones are phone trunks on the Edge group. Inherit is the default you should verify.
paras: The create-group article has you select a WebRTC or SIP phone trunk on the group. Each Edge can inherit that list. The advanced path is to ignore the group and pin trunks on one Edge’s network interface. Pinning is how a phone becomes stranded when that one Edge dies.

WebRTC phones still need a working path to the Edge or cloud media that hosts them. They are not a reason to skip the site and the location. A browser phone at home is a network design, not only a checkbox.

lessons.title: When the local Edge is offline
lessons.summary: The documented failover is another site, if that site actually has the resource.
paras: Offline, at capacity, or missing the resource: those are the only reasons the article gives for leaving the site. If site B has no trunk and no path to the agent’s station, failover has nowhere to go. Capacity is a real limit. Filling every Edge to the ceiling makes the failure path the normal path.

Cloud callers on a BYOC Cloud trunk do not use this Edge at all. An Edge outage and a cloud trunk outage are different incidents. The topology in this lab lets you toggle them separately so the two stories stay apart.

lessons.title: Choose Cloud, Premises, or both
lessons.summary: Use premises when the phones and the carrier are on your network. Use cloud when they are not. Use both only where each number has an owner.
paras: BYOC Cloud wants a public carrier and accepts internet RTP. BYOC Premises wants Edges close to phones and trunks. Genesys Cloud Voice wants neither your carrier nor your Edge for those numbers. A design that uses all three is legal and easy to mis-operate if emergency, monitoring, and the DID’s route are not labeled per number.
The quick start, the Edge group article, and the Voice region article are the three pages that justify the choice. A slide that says “hybrid” without those pages is not a design.

lessons.title: A browser phone is still a network endpoint
lessons.summary: WebRTC removes the desk set. It does not remove media engineering.
paras: The Edge group article treats WebRTC as a phone trunk. The BYOC Cloud overview treats internet RTP as something you must judge. A browser at home is both: a WebRTC endpoint whose packets cross whatever network the agent is actually on. Split tunneling, a full VPN, and a hotel network are different designs.
Do not debug a home-agent audio problem by editing Architect. Confirm the phone trunk, the Edge or cloud media the phone uses, and the path from the browser. Then look at the flow.

lessons.title: Premises turn-up checklist
lessons.summary: Group, inherit, site, trunk, failover test, emergency owner.
paras: Create the Edge group on a low-latency network. Add the phone trunk. Confirm inherit on every Edge. Put the carrier trunk where the calls are. Attach the site’s location and number plans. Run one failover test and one cloud-trunk test so you know they are different. Write the emergency owner on the same page.
None of those steps is an Architect publish. You can build the flow in parallel. You cannot let the flow be the only test.
